transcript.note: Round 1. Method: I first built the lock table from hvSegs (a V segment locks a column, an H segment locks a row), which pins 45(16,17), 23(33,23), 24(35,33), 25(35,42), 40(43,27), 22(48,23), 12(row 23), 51(14,52), 15(16,40) etc. Every unlocked endpoint of an offSeg was then examined against its own free axis, and I preferred the move that closes a whole run of segments at once rather than one segment at a time. Concretely: (a) chain 47-4-35-45 was solved jointly — 35 to (16,8) puts it on 45's locked column (V) while 4 to (11,8) lands on 35's new row (H) and simultaneously makes 47-4 a clean 8/8 diagonal, i.e. three segments fixed with two moves; (b) hub 18 was pulled down to row 10, the row 2 already sits on, which turns 2-18 into H, and its two remaining neighbours 37 and 20 were then placed on 18's new column 27 so that 18-37 and 18-20 both become V — 37 was deliberately sent SOUTH to (27,8) rather than east, because putting it east of 18 would have made segment 18-2 run straight through it and would also have wound it past 2 in the bearing order; (c) 20 to (27,17) additionally turns 23-20 into a 6/6 diagonal, and 0 followed to (24,14) to preserve its existing diagonal to 20; (d) the 13-38-12 triangle: 13 dropped to row 10 (H with 2) while keeping its 1/1 diagonal to 6 (6 and its leaf 5 moved down two rows together so the 6-5 H survives), then 38 to (38,18) makes 13-38 and 38-23 both 8/8 and 5/5 diagonals, and 12 slid along its locked row 23 to column 43 so 40-12 becomes V while 38-12 stays a 5/5 diagonal; (e) around hub 44 I moved 44 up one row to (33,29) so 36-44 becomes H, then placed 58 at (32,30) — one cell off that row on purpose, because sitting ON row 29 would have made segment 36-44 swallow 58 — which yields a 1/1 diagonal to 44 and a 3/3 diagonal to 24; (f) 16 to (25,35) trades two hopeless long segments for two exact diagonals (9/9 to 33 and 7/7 to 39); (g) leaves were the cheapest wins and were closed to H/V wherever a locked partner allowed it (21 to 47 col, 46 to row 23, 19 and 56 upgraded from 45 degrees to V, 9 slid down its locked column 43 to row 42 to meet 25's locked row); (h) 43, 7, 28 could not reach H/V within a short move, so they were placed on exact 45 degree lines instead. 34 and 53 were only moved partway this round (three cells each, to (56,27) and (49,15)) — the H/V target is one further cell and will be taken next round to keep every step short.

Round 2. Principle: finish the two-step marches started last round, then re-solve the two remaining free hubs by asking which position satisfies the MOST of their incident segments at once rather than fixing one segment at a time. (a) 34 and 53 each took the last cell of their march — 34 onto 55's locked column 57 and 53 onto 22's locked column 48 — turning both into V while their locked H partners (17-34, 54-53) survive because the moves are purely along the free axis. (b) Hub 58 was the interesting case: at (32,30) it satisfied two segments (both 45 degree, to 44 and 24) and failed two. I dropped it to (32,33), i.e. onto 24's locked row 33: that deliberately SACRIFICES the 44-58 diagonal but buys three satisfied segments instead of two, and upgrades two of them to true H/V (58-24 becomes H, 58-16 becomes H) while 36-58 becomes an exact 4/4 diagonal — H/V outranks 45 degree, so trading one diagonal for two axials is clearly positive. (c) 16 turned out to be free to SLIDE: its two diagonals (to 33 and to 39) lie on the same line c = r - 10, so any point on that line keeps both. I picked the point of that line lying on row 33 — (23,33) — which is exactly what makes 58-16 horizontal, and as a bonus 16-15 becomes a 7/7 diagonal too. Two segments gained for free, zero given up. (d) 49/52 pair: 50 is pinned to column 14 by 51-50 and 49 is pinned to row 55, so the only way to close 50-49 was to shift 49 east along its own locked row until it sat one cell diagonally from 50, taking its leaf 52 along so the 49-52 H survives. (e) 42 is 13 columns and 5 rows away from 39 with no diagonal solution, so it took the first half of a march straight up towards 39's locked row 42. The remaining offenders (36-23, 44-40, 44-24, 38-18) all have BOTH endpoints fully locked by segments that are already H/V, so touching them would cost more than it gains.

Round 3. Two principles this round. FIRST, hub 44 was re-sited by counting satisfied segments per candidate cell instead of chasing one segment: at (33,29) it satisfied 2 of its 5 edges; at (33,27) it satisfies 3 (it stays on 23's column so 44-23 remains V, it lands on 40's locked row 27 so 44-40 becomes H, and 36 followed to (26,27) — the unique cell that is both on 45's 45-degree ray and on row 27 — so 36-44 stays H and 36-58 stays an exact 6/6 diagonal). I checked that the new 44-40 run along row 27 passes no station and does not wind 40's neighbours past each other. SECOND, I started upgrading 45-degree segments to true H/V wherever a locked partner made it reachable, because H/V is the primary key and 45 degree only the secondary one — so I am willing to spend a diagonal to buy an axial: 28 to (14,49) puts it on 51's locked column (V) while staying on 27's locked row; 13 to (47,10) puts it on 6's locked column (V) at the price of the 13-38 diagonal; 52 stepped aside to (16,55) to vacate column 14, which lets 49 drop onto 50's locked column next round. Finally two marches that cannot be done in one short step: 2 and 3 are converging on a common column (39 and 30 are nine apart, so they meet in the middle over two rounds) to turn 2-3 into a vertical, and 7 is walking up column 0 towards 11's locked row 40 to turn 11-7 into a horizontal. Both marches temporarily give up a 45-degree segment; that is deliberate, the axial they buy next round outranks it. 42 completed its march onto 39's locked row 42. The four segments I am leaving alone (36-23, 44-58, 44-24, 38-18) all have both endpoints pinned by two already-axial segments each, so any move would cost more than it gains.

Round 4. Three marches land and one begins. 49 dropped onto column 14, which 52 vacated last round, so 51-50-49 now form one straight vertical run and 50-49 becomes V instead of 45 degree. 2 and 3 met on column 34 — neither could reach the other in a single short step (they were nine columns apart), so each walked half the distance while staying on its own locked row, and 2-3 is now a clean vertical of length nine; both 2's horizontals (to 13 and to 18) survive because the move was purely along row 10, and 3-1 survives because 3 stayed on row 1. 7 reached row 40 and 11-7 is now horizontal, with 7-48 still vertical on column 0. The new idea this round concerns hub 38: I had been treating it as pinned by its two 45-degree segments, but it is actually free to SLIDE along the 45-degree ray through 23 — every cell on that ray keeps 38-23 at exactly 45 degrees. Walking outwards along that ray to (43,13) puts 38 on 12's locked column 43, which converts 38-12 from 45 degree into a true vertical while 38-23 stays 45 degree, so it is a strict gain rather than a trade. (41,15) is the halfway cell of that walk; it keeps 38-23 and gives up 38-12 for one round only. The remaining offenders 36-23, 44-58, 44-24 and 38-18 are structurally blocked: each hub already satisfies three of its incident segments and every alternative cell I evaluated satisfies fewer axial segments than the current one.
